lesson.title: Handoff: Swapping Base Stations Without Dropping the Call
lesson.summary: Handoff is the process that transfers an active cellular connection from one base station to another as a device moves, using signal measurements to decide when and where to switch without interrupting service.
lesson.body:
Every cellular network is built from cells, each covering a limited geographic area from a single base station, which means a phone in a moving car will eventually leave the coverage area of the base station it started a call on. Handoff, also called handover, is the process that transfers an active connection from one base station to another as a device moves, and it has to happen without the user noticing a dropped call or a stalled download.

A handoff decision is driven by continuous signal measurements the device reports back to the network: signal strength and signal quality indicators such as RSRP (reference signal received power) and RSRQ (reference signal received quality) in LTE and 5G networks. When the network sees that a neighboring cell offers a noticeably stronger signal than the serving cell, it commands the device to retune its radio and reconnect through the new base station, then updates its internal records so that future traffic for that device routes through the new cell instead of the old one.

There are two broad strategies for the moment of transition. A hard handoff follows a break before make sequence: the connection to the old base station is torn down before the connection to the new one is established, which is simpler to implement but risks a brief gap in service if the new connection fails to form quickly. A soft handoff follows a make before break sequence instead, briefly maintaining connections to both the old and new base station at once and combining their signals, which avoids any gap but requires more radio resources and coordination; this approach was a hallmark of CDMA based networks and is less common in the OFDM based systems that LTE and 5G NR use.

Handoffs are also classified by what actually changes during the transition. An intra cell handoff moves a device between channels on the same base station, an inter cell handoff moves it to a different base station, an intra frequency handoff keeps the same carrier frequency, an inter frequency handoff changes it, and an inter RAT handoff moves the device between entirely different radio access technologies, for example dropping from 5G NR back to 4G LTE when 5G coverage runs out.

Networks also build in deliberate hysteresis, a margin that requires the target cell's signal to beat the serving cell's by a set threshold, and sometimes to stay better for a minimum dwell time, before triggering a handoff. Without that margin, a device sitting near the boundary between two cells with roughly equal signal strength could bounce back and forth between them repeatedly, a failure mode engineers call ping ponging, wasting radio resources and signaling capacity on handoffs that accomplish nothing useful for the user.

Handoff is the foundational mobility mechanism that later, more specific mobility problems build on. Mobile IP addresses a related but separate problem, keeping a device reachable at a stable IP address once its point of attachment to the network has already changed, and Wi Fi roaming is essentially the same handoff idea applied to wireless local area networks instead of cellular base stations, where a device moves between access points that share a network name instead of between cell towers that share a carrier's spectrum.
